title: Théorie des cycles algébriques : conjectures de Hodge, Tate, Lefschetz, Weil : notes manuscrites (s.d.), lettre (1965).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: X is a smooth projective surface. The objects live in N = Num(X)⊗R with the intersection form, which has signature (1, ρ−1) by Hodge index. Grothendieck works with three convex cones and their closures, interiors and duals ("polarité" means dual cone with respect to the intersection pairing).

The cones:
- P⁺ = P is the effective cone: x ∈ P iff some positive multiple nx is the class γ(C) of an effective curve C. By Riemann–Roch this is essentially iff ℓ(nx) ≥ 2 for n large.
- Q⁺ = Q is the positive cone {x² ≥ 0, x·a ≥ 0}, with a a fixed ample class ("a choisi dans Q̊, par ex. a dans R"). Its interior is Q̊ = {x² > 0, x·a ≥ 0 (in fact > 0)}.
- R is the ample cone: x ∈ R iff nx = γ(C) for some ample C.

The diagram in the upper left records the inclusions R ⊂ Q ⊂ P̄, with interiors and closures.

Key steps:
1. The boxed fact Q̊ ⊂ P. For x² > 0 and x·a > 0, Riemann–Roch gives h⁰(nx) → ∞, so nx is effective. Taking closures gives Q = cl(Q̊) ⊂ P̄, and taking interiors gives Q̊ ⊂ int P̄ = P̊.
2. By Hodge index, Q is self-dual: Q° = Q. Dualising step 1 therefore gives P̄° = P° ⊂ Q° = Q. In words, a class nonnegative on all curves has x² ≥ 0.
3. Nakai–Moishezon: x ∈ R iff x·C > 0 for all curves C and x² > 0. Hence R̄ ⊂ P° ∩ Q = P° = P̄°, i.e. nef ⊂ dual of the effective cone.
4. Conversely, int(P°) ⊂ Q̊, and one checks with Nakai's criterion that int(P°) ⊂ R. The boxed conclusion is:
   - R = int R̄ = int P° ⊂ Q̊;
   - R̄ = P° = P̄° ⊂ Q.
   This is the surface case of Kleiman's theorem: the nef cone is the closure of the ample cone and is dual to the closed cone of curves; the ample cone is the interior of the nef cone.

The open question at the bottom is whether x·P > 0 (positive on every curve) implies x ∈ R. Grothendieck's reduction:
- By Nakai, one only needs x² > 0. Since x² ≥ 0 by step 2, one only needs to exclude x² = 0.
- Take a divisor D with D² = 0 and D·C > 0 for all curves C.
- Riemann–Roch gives χ(O(nD)) = χ(O_X) + nχ(O_D), using χ(O_D) = −(D² + D·K)/2 = −D·K/2.
- For n large, h⁰(nD) ≥ χ(nD), because h²(nD) = h⁰(K − nD) = 0. Grothendieck attributes this to Mumford, linked to the 'lettre à Mumford' on the previous page.
- If χ(O_D) > 0, then nD would move in a positive-dimensional system, giving D·D > 0, a contradiction. So a counterexample must have χ(O_D) ≤ 0, i.e. D·K ≥ 0.

The thread stops there. It is precisely the situation of Mumford's counterexample, which Hartshorne published in 'Ample subvarieties' (1970). There X = P(E) over a curve of genus g ≥ 2, E stable of rank 2 and degree 0, and D = O(1). Then D² = 0, D·C > 0 for every curve, and D·K = 2g − 2 > 0, so χ(O_D) = 1 − g < 0, consistent with Grothendieck's necessary condition.

Context: the previous page treats Nakai-type ampleness criteria in all dimensions by induction, referring to a letter to Mumford.
errors: The interior of Q is written with x·a ≥ 0; strictly it should be x·a > 0, though for x² > 0 and Q connected this is harmless.

The final question is left open. As literally stated (x·C > 0 for every curve C) the answer is negative by Mumford's example; only the version 'positive on P̄ minus {0}' (Kleiman's criterion) is true. The page derives only the necessary condition χ(O_D) ≤ 0.
The reading 'Propo de Grothe' in the upper right is uncertain and may not be a self-citation.

ideas.what: Interior of the positive cone lies in the effective cone, via Riemann–Roch on surfaces
ideas.modern_name: Positive cone contained in the big/pseudo-effective cone

ideas.what: Self-duality of the positive cone Q° = Q from Hodge index, and dualisation giving P° ⊂ Q
ideas.modern_name: Hodge index theorem / nef classes have nonnegative self-intersection
ideas.usually_credited_to: Hodge, Segre; Grothendieck 1958 (algebraic proof of index theorem); Kleiman 1966
ideas.where_published: Grothendieck, 'Sur une note de Mattuck–Tate' (Crelle 1958), for the index theorem

ideas.what: Closure of the ample cone equals the dual of the effective cone; ample cone equals the interior of the nef cone
ideas.modern_name: Kleiman's ampleness criterion / nef cone duality
ideas.usually_credited_to: Kleiman, 'Toward a numerical theory of ampleness' (Annals 1966)

ideas.what: Reduction of 'positive on all curves implies ample' to excluding D² = 0, with the necessary condition χ(O_D) ≤ 0 (D·K ≥ 0) for a counterexample
ideas.modern_name: Strictly nef but not ample divisors (Mumford's example)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Mumford, published in Hartshorne, 'Ample subvarieties of algebraic varieties' (1970)

missed.claim: Grothendieck independently set up the cone/duality picture (effective, positive, ample cones with closures, interiors and duals) on a surface, apparently contemporaneous with Kleiman's 1965–66 work. This is a small historical datum on the genesis of Kleiman's numerical theory of ampleness and Grothendieck's influence on it.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical credit only; the mathematics is standard (Kleiman 1966, Mumford's example).

missed.claim: Open question whether a strictly nef class is ample on a surface, reduced to classes with D² = 0 and D·K ≥ 0. Settled negatively by Mumford's ruled-surface example.
missed.quote: Question xP>0 ⇒? x ∈ R ... on doit donc avoir χ(D) ≤ 0
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Nothing new: the answer is known. It does show Grothendieck isolating the canonical-class sign condition that Mumford's example satisfies.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a careful but standard derivation of cone duality on surfaces and of the strict-nef question, all now in Kleiman 1966 and Mumford/Hartshorne. Its only interest is as a trace of Grothendieck's involvement in the numerical theory of ampleness.
transcription_corrections: Q^{\#} and P^{\#} appear to be the same objects as Q^{+} and P^{+}; the superscript is a hand-drawn '+' or '#' symbol.
'[a choisi dans \mathring{Q}^{\#}], par ex. a dans R]' — the bracketed note specifies the reference ample class a.
'j'en dis rien (inégalités)' is likely 'je dis (via inégalités)' — uncertain.
In the bottom lines, 'tel que D²=0' belongs to 'On peut supposer que x provient de D diviseur ... tel que D²=0'.
'R = \mathring{\overline{K}}' in the box should read R = \mathring{\overline{R}}.
